I farm by what has held up on our side of Hebei, not by fancy talk. I have 60 mu, but my labor is not all in the field because some people in the family work outside, so I will keep the main land in the steadiest pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That gives me grain in both seasons, and with well water I can keep it from getting stuck at the key times. I will put 30 mu into wheat first, then after wheat harvest I will seed summer maize on that same 30 mu. The other 30 mu I will split between spring peanut and cotton. Peanut is good for cash and does not need as much water as wheat, and cotton can still make money here, but cotton eats more labor and more sprays, so I will not make it too big.

For fertilizer, I do not like to cut too hard. If I save a little fertilizer and lose yield, that loss is bigger than the saving. So on wheat and maize I will keep the rate solid. On peanut I will not push too much nitrogen because then it grows vines and not pods; I will give it more phosphorus and some potassium. Cotton I will feed steadily because if it runs short later, bolls suffer. For tillage, I will plough the peanut and cotton ground because that land does better loosened up, and for the wheat-maize land I will use rotary for wheat and mostly no-tillage or simple direct seeding for maize after the wheat comes off, to save time. For water, wheat gets the most attention because one missed irrigation can cost a lot. Sprays I count by what usually happens here: wheat a few times, maize less, peanut middle, cotton the most. That is how I will manage it this year.
